newsitem.title: USA: Texas auto rental group joins fight vs stadium.
newsitem.headline: Texas auto rental group joins fight vs stadium.

text.p: An association of auto rental companies has fired the latest shot in battle over a stadium financing proposal on Harris County, Texas' November election ballot.

The Texas Car and Truck Rental and Leasing Association (CATRALA) held a press conference Tuesday announcing its opposition to the stadium plan called "Proposition 1," which it says will mean a five percent tax increase on tourists and local consumers who rent cars and trucks in Harris County.
The car and truck tax increase is one method the county is contemplating to help finance a roughly $265 million proposed baseball stadium in downtown Houston.

John Ebeling, a director and past president of Texas CATRALA, on Wednesday said claims by the Proposition 1 supporters that tourists will bear most of the new tax costs are incorrect. A Texas CATRALA survey indicated that close to 60 percent of all cars rented in Harris County are rented by residents.

Dan McClung, a political consultant hired by a committee called Harris County Citizens for Proposition 1, said the county will try to minimize the proposed tax's impact on Harris County residents by basing it on length of stay.
Shorter stays tend to indicate use by business travelers, while longer use typically indicates local residents' use.

"There will be occasions when the tax might be applied to a Harris County resident, but the idea is to minimize that situation," McClung said. Florida has used auto rental taxes to finance sports facilities there, he said.
In addition, the new stadium would likely mean an economic boost and increased auto rentals, he said.

"We would expect businesses would do a lot better if we had the stadium and the economic development that it would create," McClung said. "We expect that there will be a lot more car rental use if we have the stadium and the business and the economic generator that comes out of that. And so the likelihood is everybody will do better."
While vistors may have to pay slightly higher taxes, McClung said he doubts the increase will deter them from coming to town.
But Ebeling disagreed.
"We rent a lot of cars to local residents whose cars are in the shop for a day or two," he said. "You can't determine or discriminate by the number of days it is rented."
Far from increasing business, the new tax could hurt it, Ebeling said.

A "fabulous" place to live, Houston is no tourist destination, he said. From a business standpoint, Houston's lure as a convention destination could suffer under the auto tax plan. Customers renting at airports already pay a 16 percent tax, and the five percent additional tax would bring that to 21 percent, he said.

Proposition 1 would authorize Harris County "to establish and operate new or renovated stadiums, arenas and other facilities for professional baseball and football teams." Key to the proposal however is that "no county real or personal property taxes (would be) spent to acquire, construct, or equip these facilities."
Opponents of the measure, however, disagree.

"Don't be fooled; the ballot language does allow property taxes to be used for stadium maintenance and operation, or, worst of all, possibly to guarantee debt," Harris County Treasurer Don Sumners wrote recently in a statement called "The Score on Stadiums."

Sally Lehr, media liason for Harris County Judge Robert Eckels, said a newly created sports authority, not the county, would issue the bonds. The sports authority would also seek insurance on the bonds at issuance as a safeguard in case the revenue stream falls short.
According to McClung, bonds issued to pay for the roughly $265 million baseball stadium would be paid for with revenue generated from car and truck rentals and other new revenue streams.

The county also plans a $200 million overhaul of the existing Astrodome stadium and some rodeo facilities, but a hotel-motel tax already in place, not auto rental taxes, would be used for service debt issued for the additional improvments.
--Kathie O'Donnell, 212-859-1655
